sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Thinking in objects is like seeing the world as LEGO blocks - everything fits together! You'll learn how to design programs by modeling real-world things as objects.

• How to break problems into objects
• Why objects make code more organized
• How to design classes that work together

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you're building a car. Instead of thinking about every single bolt and wire, you think about the big pieces: engine, wheels, seats. That's object-oriented thinking!

Objects are like those car parts - they bundle data (like size, color) with actions (like drive, brake).

• **Objects** = Things that exist (a specific car, a bank account)
• **Classes** = Blueprints for objects (the design of a car model)
• **Methods** = What objects can do (accelerate, withdraw money)

For example, a `Dog` class might have:
• Data: name, breed, age
• Actions: bark(), eat(), sleep()

sections.title: 📊 Visual Simulation
sections.content: Step-by-step visualization of how Thinking in Objects works:

steps.title: Identify the Objects
steps.description: Look at the problem. What real-world things are involved? For a library system, you might see: Books, Members, Librarians.

steps.title: Define Their Properties
steps.description: What data does each object need? Books need titles, Members need names, etc.

steps.title: Add Behaviors
steps.description: What can each object do? Books can be checked out, Members can borrow books.

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Objects combine data + actions (like a car has wheels + can drive)
✓ Classes are templates, objects are actual instances (like cookie cutter vs cookies)
✓ Good objects model real-world things naturally
✓ Objects interact by calling each other's methods
✓ Start design by identifying nouns (objects) and verbs (methods)

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Keep objects focused on one purpose
donts: Don't make objects do too much (like a Swiss Army knife)
Don't create classes for things that aren't real objects
sections.protip: If you can say 'a [class name] can [method name]', it's probably well-designed!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Thinking in Objects used in real apps?

examples.how: Products, Carts, and Users are all objects that interact (e.g., a Cart object holds Product objects)
Characters, weapons, and levels are objects with properties (health, damage) and actions (attack, move)
Accounts, Transactions, and Customers are objects with methods like deposit() and withdraw()

problem.description:
Design a simple `Student` class for a school system. A student should have:
• Name and ID
• Ability to enroll in courses
• Track their grades
hints: What data does a student need? (name, id, list of courses)
What actions can a student take? (enroll, get grades)
How would you store multiple courses?
problem.explanation: This solution models a student with basic properties and methods. The `enroll()` method adds courses, and `setGrade()` updates grades. In real apps, you'd use more advanced data structures!

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Design starts with identifying real-world things
📌 Practice by modeling everyday objects (phones, pets, etc.)
📌 Ready to learn about class relationships next!
